definitions.meaning: A measure of the average kinetic energy of the molecules of a substance: average KE = (3/2) k T, so temperature is proportional to that average when T is in kelvin.
The model that treats a gas as a huge number of tiny particles in constant random motion, colliding elastically with each other and with the walls; pressure is the effect of those wall collisions.
Energy transferred from a hotter body to a colder one because of their temperature difference; it is a transfer, not something a body contains.
The total kinetic energy of the molecules from their random motion plus their potential energy from intermolecular forces - the sum over every molecule, not the average.
Heat transfer through a material by particle collisions and vibrations passed on atom by atom, helped in metals by free electrons, with no bulk movement of the material.
Heat transfer in a fluid by bulk movement: warmed fluid expands, becomes less dense and rises, while cooler denser fluid sinks, setting up a circulating loop.
Heat transfer by electromagnetic waves (mainly infrared), needing no medium; a black body radiates power P = sigma A T^4 by the Stefan-Boltzmann law.
A gas that obeys pV = nRT at all temperatures and pressures: its particles have negligible volume, exert no intermolecular forces except during collisions, and collide elastically.

mechanismSteps: Temperature: molecules jiggle faster when hotter - turning the dial from 300 K to 600 K makes the same molecules jiggle harder, because their average kinetic energy (3/2) k T has doubled.
Conduction: heat travels atom by atom - hot-end atoms vibrate strongly, collide with neighbours and pass the energy along the lattice (and, in metals, through free electrons) until the far end warms.
Convection: the fluid loops - fluid heated at the bottom expands, grows less dense and rises, while cooler denser fluid sinks, so the circulating loop carries the heat around.
Radiation: hotter means more packets, faster - every body radiates, and by P = sigma A T^4 doubling the kelvin temperature multiplies the radiated power by 16.

Misconception: a common mistake about heat and temperature - heat is the total over all molecules while temperature is the average per molecule, so a small hot cup can beat a big warm bucket on temperature while losing on total heat.
objectives: State that temperature is proportional to the average kinetic energy of the molecules, and calculate average KE = (3/2) k T
Use the ideal-gas law pV = nRT and the fixed-volume rule p proportional to T, always in kelvin
Distinguish conduction, convection and radiation, and explain each one at the particle level

title: JC H2 physics — thermal: kinetic theory, gas laws and temperature

trap.explanation: The slip: Hotter means faster, so every molecule feels faster. The fix: Hotter means a higher average: the whole spread of speeds shifts up, but some molecules still crawl. Temperature tracks the average kinetic energy only, so a hotter gas is one whose speed distribution has shifted up as a whole - never one where every single molecule has sped up.
trap.misconception: In a hotter gas every molecule moves faster.

workedExample: Calculate the average kinetic energy of a gas molecule at 300 K, and again at 600 K. (Boltzmann constant k = 1.38 x 10^-23 J K^-1) Step 1: average KE = (3/2) k T = 1.5 x 1.38 x 10^-23 x 300 = 6.21 x 10^-21 J. Step 2: at 600 K, average KE = 1.5 x 1.38 x 10^-23 x 600 = 1.24 x 10^-20 J. Step 3: doubling the kelvin temperature exactly doubles the average, from 6.21 x 10^-21 J to 1.24 x 10^-20 J. These are averages over a spread of molecular speeds: at 600 K most molecules are faster than at 300 K, but some are still slow.
